How many watts does a TV use, and how long will a power station run one?

Power basics Updated 2026-08-08

There is no single answer, and the US certified television dataset is explicit about why: measured on-mode power tracks screen size. It averages 31.7 W across the 30-to-34-inch sets in that dataset, 107.5 W across the 54-to-66-inch class most households own, and 171.2 W across sets of 74 inches and larger.

Any of those sits far inside the continuous output of every machine in this library, so the question is never whether a power station runs a television — it is for how long. Against the three records whose published fields allow the division, a 55-to-65-inch set runs 2.1 h on the smallest and 14 h on the largest.

What the set costs for the nineteen hours a day nobody is watching it.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · LED TV record · ENERGY STAR certified dataset

The spread inside a single size band is why this page gives you four numbers instead of one. Sixty-five sets of roughly the same size, taken under the same test procedure, still span nearly a factor of two. The record’s own note names the variable: picture brightness and the kind of content playing, not the temperature of the room. So treat the band as a starting point and your own set as somewhere inside it — and if you still have the manual, its rating plate beats every figure on this page.

Every annual figure you have read assumes five hours a day

A television’s energy label is not an observation of your living room. The US Department of Energy’s test procedure for televisions — 10 CFR 430, Appendix H — fixes the usage pattern that turns a bench measurement into a yearly number: 5 h a day in on mode and 19 h a day in standby. Every “kWh per year” anyone quotes for a television carries that assumption inside it, whether or not the page says so.

The published year, and the same year rebuilt

The second row is the first row’s own arithmetic run in reverse. The two agree to within half a percent, which is how you can tell the five-hour assumption is load-bearing rather than decorative.

Standby is not what empties the battery

A set left in networked standby draws 0.5 W, so an overnight nineteen hours of it costs about 9.1 Wh — the record’s standby figure multiplied by the same nineteen hours the test procedure uses, our multiplication. Next to a single hour of watching that is a rounding error. Unplugging the television overnight is sound housekeeping on a grid bill; during an outage it changes almost nothing.

Questions people ask

How many watts does a TV use?
It depends on the screen, and the certified US dataset splits it by size: about 31.7 W across seven 30-to-34-inch sets, 107.5 W across sixty-five 54-to-66-inch sets, and 171.2 W across fifty-one sets of 74 inches or more. Individual sets inside the 54-to-66-inch band alone run from 72.52 W to 134.53 W, so use the band as a starting point and your own rating plate if you still have it.
How long will a power station run a TV?
On the three records here whose published fields allow the division, a 55-to-65-inch set runs 2.1 hours on a 300 Wh class machine, 7.1 hours on a 1,000 Wh class one and 14 hours on a 2,000 Wh class one. Those hours already include each machine’s own self-consumption, which is why they are shorter than capacity divided by watts.
Why does my TV’s label say a different number of kWh per year?
Because the annual figure is computed rather than observed. The US test procedure for televisions (10 CFR 430, Appendix H) assumes 5 hours a day in on mode and 19 hours in standby. Multiply this record’s measured 107.5 W and 0.48 W by those hours across 365 days and you land within half a percent of the certified annual figure — so a household that watches more or less than five hours a day will not match the label.
